A daily return multiple is not a holding-period multiple: compare two paths with the same index finish

Use original synthetic daily returns to compare smooth and paired-swing paths, ideal daily leverage and a separate multiple-of-full-period arithmetic reference.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare ideal daily-multiple compounding on two synthetic paths with the same index endpoint

Interactive planning lab

Ideal daily-multiple account: smooth-path final capital$10,000
Ideal daily-multiple account: paired-swing final capital$8,323.59
Paired-swing capital minus the full-period arithmetic reference-$1,676.41

Original deterministic compounding illustration, not a real index, ETF, backtest, simulation of likely prices or investment recommendation. Both synthetic benchmark paths start at 100 and finish at 100.00 after 20 numbered trading days. Each account starts with the same CAD capital and is assumed to deliver exactly the entered multiple of each benchmark’s simple daily return, compounded on its own changing capital. The smooth path has a constant daily log return; the other adds and subtracts log(1 + swing parameter) in each two-day pair, so both benchmark endpoints match. The swing parameter is neither an annualized volatility estimate nor symmetric plus/minus simple returns. All permitted daily account factors remain positive. The full-period arithmetic reference is starting capital × (1 + multiple × complete-window index return); it is not a product return promise or modeled investable portfolio. Fees, financing, tracking error, tax, distributions, trading spreads, intraday purchase timing and external cash flows are excluded. Reordering the same set of daily returns changes intermediate values but not either final product in this cash-flow-free model. Different paired-swing settings change the return set rather than merely reorder it.

The central idea

Compound the stated daily return rule across the actual window. The index’s final percentage alone does not determine an ideal daily-multiple account’s final capital.

01

Keep the objective’s time window beside its multiple

A statement about twice an index’s daily return describes one daily calculation. It does not promise twice the index’s return over a month or another holding period. Compounding acts on the account’s changing capital after each day.

The SEC staff’s updated investor bulletin on leveraged and inverse ETFs, dated 29 August 2023, explains that daily objectives can diverge substantially from a multiple of the benchmark’s longer-period performance. It also discusses risks and the importance of reading the specific product’s disclosures.

This page isolates the arithmetic with an ideal account and original synthetic benchmark paths. It does not model any actual ETF or recommend a product. The account is assumed to deliver the chosen positive multiple exactly every day before fees, financing costs, taxes or tracking differences. Only 1x, 2x and 3x positive daily multiples are offered.

02

Construct two benchmark paths with an identical complete-window return

The default window contains ten two-day pairs, or twenty numbered hypothetical trading days. Both benchmarks start at 100 and finish at 100. The selected complete-window return is therefore zero.

The smooth path has zero return each day. The paired path rises 10% on the first day of each pair and then falls by about 9.0909% on the next. Its level moves from 100 to 110 and back to 100 before beginning the next pair.

The second move is not −10%. A 10% gain followed by a 10% loss would finish below the original level, so it would not provide the matched endpoint used here. The paired path instead multiplies by 1.10 and then by 1 ÷ 1.10.

The first chart shows benchmark points, not dollars invested or an actual index history. The swing parameter is a construction input. It is not an estimate of annual market volatility, a symmetric plus/minus daily return or a probability of a future outcome.

03

Apply the daily multiple to the account’s own current capital

Each account begins with CAD 10,000. Under the ideal 2x daily rule, the paired path’s first +10% benchmark day gives the account +20%, taking it to CAD 12,000.

The next benchmark move is approximately −9.0909%, so the account’s second-day return is approximately −18.1818%. That loss applies to CAD 12,000, leaving CAD 9,818.18. The benchmark has returned to 100, but the daily-multiple account has not returned to CAD 10,000.

The exact account multiplier for this two-day pair is 1.20 × (1 − 2/11) = 54/55. The daily rule has been followed perfectly in the illustration. There is no tracking error or fee needed to produce the difference.

The second chart repeats that rule each day: next capital equals current capital × (1 + daily multiple × benchmark daily return). A separate simple multiplication of the final index return is a different calculation.

04

Repeating the original pairs compounds the difference

After ten identical default pairs, the ideal 2x account finishes at CAD 10,000 × (54/55)10 = approximately CAD 8,323.59. That is about 16.76% below its starting capital, while the constructed benchmark finishes unchanged.

The smooth benchmark has zero return each day, so its ideal 2x account remains at CAD 10,000. The two accounts therefore have different final capital despite benchmark paths with the same initial and final levels.

The endpoint bars also include a full-period arithmetic reference: starting capital × (1 + selected multiple × complete-window benchmark return). At the default zero index return, that reference is CAD 10,000.

The reference is not a forecast, a fund promise or a modeled investable portfolio. It is shown to identify the calculation that would be incorrect if substituted for the daily-compounding rule. The reported signed gap subtracts this reference from the paired-path result.

05

Divergence does not mean the daily result is always below the simple reference

Change the window to one two-day pair, the complete-window benchmark return to +20%, and the paired swing to zero. Both days then have the same benchmark return of approximately 9.5445%, because their two growth factors must multiply to 1.20.

The ideal 2x account compounds to about CAD 14,182.20, a return of approximately 41.82%. The full-period arithmetic reference is CAD 10,000 × (1 + 2 × 20%) = CAD 14,000. In that different constructed path, daily compounding finishes above the simple reference.

The lesson is the difference in calculation windows, not a claim that every path creates a fixed loss called a daily-reset fee. The matrix varies the daily multiple and paired swing while preserving the selected benchmark endpoint and number of days. Its cells have no probability weights and estimate no future returns.

At 1x, compounding the same daily benchmark returns reproduces the benchmark’s full-period return in this ideal no-cost model. Near-zero comparison differences caused solely by floating-point precision are displayed as zero.

06

Changing the daily-return set is different from changing its order

The smooth and paired paths do not merely rearrange the same returns. They use different daily-return sets with a common cumulative benchmark result. Changing the swing parameter changes those returns.

For a fixed set of daily simple returns, this model’s final account is starting capital multiplied by the product of all factors (1 + multiple × daily return). Reordering the factors does not change that final product. The same is true of the benchmark’s daily growth factors.

Reordering can still change intermediate account levels and drawdowns. Also, contributions, withdrawals, fees that depend on the path, altered exposure rules and other product mechanics can change the problem. None is included here. The order-invariance statement applies only to this fixed-multiple, cash-flow-free illustration.

This distinction prevents a matched-endpoint chart from being presented as evidence that simply reversing an unchanged return list must change its final compounded value.

07

Use the actual objective and cash deadline in a financial plan

A goal budget needs the capital available when the bill is due, rather than a daily multiple copied onto an assumed annual index return. An index scenario alone is insufficient to calculate the result of a product with a different reset window.

For a real product, its objective, reset convention, costs, trading conditions and disclosures need to be read directly. This page adds no product fees or financing estimate and assumes exact daily tracking. Intraday entry, distributions, external cash flows and taxes are outside its scope.

The synthetic daily moves are deliberately simple teaching cases. They are not representative volatility statistics, historical performance or expected market behaviour. The related leverage-loss guide examines capital exposed to an asset decline; the deadline guide considers a separate bill date. Those planning questions remain relevant even when a daily-compounding formula is understood.
